title: The media industry is becoming a prediction economy
excerpt: For two decades, media and advertising ran on attention. Impressions, reach and clicks...
summary: Databricks argues that media and advertising are shifting from competing for attention to relying on predictions about what audiences will do. The teaser is short, so details of how this works are not covered here.

title: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
excerpt: Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser , or send data to other command-line programs while they run. In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand() . Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done: You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin . The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends. In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send() . Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit: For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process() . Read the Sandbox documentation to get started. Read more
summary: Vercel Sandbox commands can now receive typed input while they run, through a feature called stdin. This lets programs in a sandbox exchange messages with other tools, such as browser helper servers, while they are working.

title: Run Scale AI’s AgentEnv evals on Vercel Sandbox
excerpt: AgentEnv , Scale AI's framework for testing agents against tasks and scoring their results, now runs on Vercel Sandbox . The Vercel provider ships in AgentEnv 0.9.1334 and later, and runs the agent and its task environment in separate Sandboxes. Try the AgentEnv example to run an evaluation on Vercel Sandbox and inspect the task’s score and the agent’s recorded actions. After completing the setup guide , run this command from the cloned repository. It uses your existing Vercel CLI login: Replace YOUR_TEAM with your Vercel team slug and YOUR_PROJECT with an existing project name. Learn more in the Sandbox ecosystem documentation . Read more
summary: Scale AI's tool for testing AI agents on tasks now runs on Vercel Sandbox, a separate isolated environment for each part of the test. Users can follow a setup guide and run an example to see how the agent scored and what it did.

title: GPT-6.1 Terra now available on AI Gateway
excerpt: GPT-6.1 Terra from OpenAI is now available on AI Gateway . GPT-6.1 Terra is a fast model for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, and it improves on the previous Terra model in visual reasoning, factual accuracy, and coding. It suits high-volume work in documents and desktop apps, such as filling out forms, interpreting technical drawings, or entering invoice details into accounting software. OpenAI still recommends its larger GPT-6 models for the most complex coding tasks. The model accepts text and images and returns text, with a context window of more than 1M tokens. It supports configurable reasoning effort , structured outputs , tool calling, and implicit and explicit prompt caching . For latency-sensitive work, fast mode is available as openai/gpt-6.1-terra-fast . GPT-6.1 Terra works with the AI SDK , the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API , the Responses API , and coding agents connected to AI Gateway. Use openai/gpt-6.1-terra as the model name: To use it in Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup: Then select openai/gpt-6.1-terra in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details. Try GPT-6.1 Terra in the model playground . AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting , Zero Data Retention support , budgets for API keys , routing rules , and more. AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests. You can view all language models available on AI Gateway. Read more
summary: Vercel's AI Gateway now offers OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast model that handles images and text well, good for form filling, reading drawings, and entering invoices. It is not the best pick for the hardest coding tasks, where OpenAI's larger models are recommended.

excerpt: Fanatics uses OpenAI to help fans complete their game-day outfits with Shop the Look. Testing across roughly 30,000 MLB products showed 10% higher engagement.

excerpt: Explore OpenAI Signals data on 165 work activities across nearly 100 countries, revealing how people use ChatGPT for work and how usage changes over time.

title: Multi‑Ratio Video Resizing for Mobile Feed and Marketing
excerpt: Serdar Cellat , Yuchen Xie , Bernadette Marcu , Blaid Burgess , Cody Jarrett , Carlos Pereira , Qing Shi , Samuel Carvajal , Manuel Pamplona , Dorothy Jung , Feiko Ritsema , Benjamin Klein , Alex Woo , Eugene Lok , Anna Pulido , Rebecka Swe , Sanford Holsapple Introduction Clips in the Netflix mobile app. At Netflix, a crucial part of our mission is ensuring our content looks stunning on any device. Vertical formats are increasingly important for Netflix, as we have 1.2B followers across our social media accounts, and have recently rolled out Clips , our vertical video feed in the Netflix mobile app. Traditionally, creating vertical assets meant editors and producers manually reframed horizontal videos in editing tools, a process that doesn’t scale as our catalog and use cases grow. To support both our in‑app feed and external marketing campaigns at scale, we built an automated multi‑ratio video cropping system, tightly integrated into our internal production tools, that can generate high‑quality vertical and other aspect‑ratio variants with minimal manual effort. Our Video Resizing Approach Converting cinematic 16:9 footage into mobile‑friendly aspect ratios takes more than a simple center crop. Filmmaking often involves dynamic character blocking and complex camera movement. We need an intelligent “virtual camera” that can follow the key action, respond to how each scene is composed, and produce crops that feel as intentional as the original shot. We address this challenge by framing video resizing as a tracking and temporal optimization problem. Our pipeline processes each asset in three main stages, designed to produce 9:16, 4:5, and 1:1 crops in a single pass, without incurring additional computational overhead. An overview of the three-stage process converting horizontal footage into mobile aspect ratios. Shot Detection and Splitting First, we segment the video into atomic shots using a neural‑network–based shot boundary detector. In many cases, shots contain multiple characters conversing on opposite sides of the frame. To better handle these scenarios, we use an Active Speaker Detection based approach to logically split a single continuous shot into multiple sub‑shots. This allows our virtual camera to cut and re-focus on different speakers as the conversation flows. Our Active Speaker Detection leverages an internal face detector and LipFlap to reliably identify active speakers in both live‑action and animated titles. Shot splitting via Active Speaker Detection. The magenta box represents the dynamic vertical crop. Focus Region Discovery Once shots and sub‑shots are defined, we identify the most important region in each frame. We combine face detections with visual saliency maps to filter and prioritize the faces that should be in focus. In scenes with multiple characters, we further rank faces using signals such as active speaker status and relative size. Our model aggregates these cues with shot‑level content understanding to establish a continuous “focus region” for the virtual camera. Blue box shows the focus region around the primary character for reframing. Temporal Reframing Once we’ve established the focus region, the next challenge is deciding how the crop should move over time. Tracking the focus region on a strict frame-by-frame basis would produce a shaky, distracting viewing experience, so we apply a set of heuristics that consider how the focus region moves over the course of a shot. When its displacement is small, we lock a static crop window that consistently covers the relevant area. When there is significant motion, we compute a dynamic tracking window and smooth its path so that any panning feels intentional and cinematic. The vertical crop (magenta box) follows the character’s movement with a smooth panning path. Tooling and Workflow Integration We integrated the resizing algorithm directly into our internal Clips tool, so editors and producers can access it as part of their existing workflow. The
summary: Netflix built an automatic tool that turns wide movie scenes into vertical and square versions for its mobile Clips feed and marketing. It finds the main characters, follows who is speaking, and moves the crop smoothly, so editors no longer reframe videos by hand.

title: Making Failure Diagnosis Reliable with Pensive AI
excerpt: By Praneeth Yenugutala , Victor Dusa , Anastasia Samoilova , Megan Ren , Justin Wei , Marcelo Mayworm At Netflix, data and machine learning practitioners run millions of workloads each day across orchestration systems and compute engines such as Titus, Spark, Trino, and Druid. On peak days, roughly 100,000 workloads fail. When workloads fail, the failure itself is only the beginning. Someone still needs to find the useful signal in several logs, decide whether the cause sits in their code or the platform, and determine whether to retry, reconfigure, or escalate. Even a small share of difficult failures can consume engineering time, waste compute, and interrupt critical data pipelines. Our first answer to that problem was Pensive , an auto-diagnosis and remediation system in Netflix’s data platform. Pensive collected logs from failed workloads, used regular expressions and hand-authored Java rules to extract and classify errors, then passed retry or remediation guidance to products such as Maestro . It made ~ 50% of failures self-service and, in some cases, automatic. Rules work well for known patterns, but their coverage grows only when someone recognizes a new failure mode, understands the logs, writes a rule, and keeps it current as engines and log formats change. Over one three-month period, Pensive processed roughly seven million job-failure classifications, yet about half fell into the unknown bucket. We needed a way to expand coverage without giving up the deterministic parts of Pensive that already worked. To solve this ambiguous and complex problem at Netflix scale, we invested in Pensive AI to add AI-assisted error extractions and focused diagnosis and remediation guidance to our data and ML practitioners. The goal was not simply to place a model in front of a large collection of logs. We needed bounded extraction, predictable evaluation inputs, responsive product behavior, and quality checks that could follow the system from local development through production. Those requirements shaped every layer of the design, which we will discuss in this blog. Pensive AI wraps AI around deterministic processes, which gives broader coverage, low latency, controlled AI costs, and easier maintenance across the software development lifecycle. Building on this foundation, we plan to explore more agentic debugging experiences, as Part 6 describes. Early results are encouraging. AI error extraction now covers 100% of failures, including the failures that legacy Pensive classified as unknown. Failed step attempts where no one used Pensive AI averaged 321% more manual debug-log exploration actions than attempts where someone did (an observational comparison, not a causal claim). Figure 1. Pensive AI architecture. Always-on error extraction and on-demand debugging complement each other and share log sources, the LLM gateway, tracing, and the cache. Archived logs feed offline evals and release gates. The two paths complement each other. Error extraction improves an existing capability and is always on. It lets the user of a failed Maestro workload quickly check the parts of the logs that may point to an immediate root cause. It has low latency and low cost, and it can help in a large share of cases. On-demand debugging enables a new capability. It looks at symptoms across the logs and adds the LLM’s own knowledge and reasoning for a deeper analysis, at slightly higher latency and cost. Extraction gives a fast first look at every failure, and on-demand debugging triggered by the user goes deeper when that first look is not enough. Part 1: Finding the useful errors Legacy Pensive rules are precise, but each one captures a particular log shape. A simplified rule looks like this: - name: SparkContainerOOM logSource: GENIE_STDERR restartable: false regex: "Container.*is running beyond physical memory limits.*Killing container" summary: Spark AM container runs out of memory With Pensive AI, we wanted to find useful errors that had no correspond
summary: Netflix built Pensive AI, which uses AI to read logs from failed data jobs and point out the likely cause. Before, its rule-based system left about half of failures unexplained; now AI extraction covers every failure.

title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
excerpt: At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark , and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster . Highlights IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners. Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster , plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI. Ethernet for scale-up : Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1. OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer . v1.0 spec submitted to OCP. MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks , now going open source. We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! Keynote and Executive Sessions Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale ( video ) AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together. Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking ( video ) AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls. Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era ( video ) Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions. Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch ( video ) IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity. Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T ( video ) A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T. Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy, Hardware Engineer, Meta; Siamak Amiralizadeh, Optical Engineer, Meta; Xu Wang, Hardware Engineer, Meta Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale ( video ) At AI scale, the per-module retimer DSP is a repeated tax in power, heat, and cost across millions of links — but removing it moves equalization and triage onto the host. This talk answers whether linear optics can match retimed reliability at fleet scale. Speakers: Amin Yekani, Optical Engineer, Meta; Qing Wang, Optical Engineer, Meta Large-Scale Deployment of 800G AECs in Meta Data Centers ( video ) The economics of A
summary: At a 2026 industry summit, Meta shared new networking gear and designs for its AI data centers, including a liquid-cooled switch rack and a new open standard for switch software. The goal is to connect huge numbers of AI chips faster, using open technology that other companies can also use.

title: Unifying Edge AI: How Coral NPU’s open standard brings portable, energy-viable intelligence from model to silicon
excerpt: Google Research has completed the 32-bit open-source Coral NPU RISC-V architecture with the introduction of its Matrix Execution Unit, which delivers up to 1 TOPS while targeting 10 mW average power for edge inference. Alongside this architecture, the release of the v1.0 open-source IREE/MLIR compiler allows developers to take models from JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow straight to Coral NPU hardware without writing custom assembly. Developers can now prototype and deploy these multimodal edge applications using new hardware options like the Synaptics Astra SR200 MCU series and globally available Coralboard devkits.12
summary: Google released an open-source chip design for small devices like wearables, able to run AI tasks on very little battery power. Developers can now take AI models built with common tools and run them on this chip without writing low-level code.

title: Three layers, one repo: a tour of google/adk-recipes
excerpt: The google/adk-recipes repository unifies Agent Development Kit (ADK) resources into three structured layers—core/, plugins/, and contrib/—serving as a single source of truth for building AI agents. Developers can leverage reference patterns, install modular vertical skills (such as retail product search and virtual try-on) directly into their coding assistants, and deploy production-ready services across multiple languages. This cohesive structure streamlines the entire workflow from initial scaffolding to full deployment on Google Cloud infrastructure.
summary: Google released a repository called adk-recipes that organizes resources for building AI agents into three folders: core, plugins, and contrib. It includes reusable examples and ready-made skills that developers can add to their coding tools and deploy to Google Cloud.

title: The Outer Loop, Insights First: An Ambient Quality Agent That Diagnoses Your Production Agent
excerpt: How do you keep improving an AI agent after the first 80%, once it serves real production traffic and silent quality regressions return HTTP 200 OK? We are open-sourcing AQuA (Ambient Quality Agent), a reference implementation that runs beside your production agent in Google Cloud, sweeps and verifies failure clusters against conversation transcripts, and diagnoses root causes anchored to the exact deployed source snapshot.
summary: Google has released AQuA, a free tool that watches a live AI assistant and finds the causes of quality problems. It checks saved conversations for patterns of failure and points to the exact code version that caused them, so teams can fix AI agents that give wrong answers without showing any error.

title: Supercharge your development with the Google Developer Knowledge API ecosystem
excerpt: Google is launching the Developer Knowledge API and MCP Server in public preview. This new toolset provides a canonical, machine-readable way for AI assistants and agentic platforms to search and retrieve up-to-date documentation across Firebase, Google Cloud, Android, and more. By using the official MCP server, developers can connect tools directly to Google’s documentation corpus, ensuring that AI-generated code and guidance are based on authoritative, real-time context.
summary: Google has launched a public preview of a Developer Knowledge API and a server that lets AI assistants search and pull up-to-date Google developer docs for Firebase, Google Cloud, and Android. This aims to make AI-written code and advice rely on official, current documentation.

title: Streaming comes to API Gateway: real-time and AI-ready APIs, without changing your spec
excerpt: API Gateway now supports real-time streaming—including Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, gRPC, and chunked transfer encoding—in Public Preview without requiring changes to your existing API specifications. This update allows developers to route long-lived, bi-directional streams and AI workloads directly through the gateway while maintaining consistent authentication, rate limiting, and observability. Additionally, gateways now feature deterministic default hostnames, simplifying environment provisioning and infrastructure-as-code management.
summary: API Gateway now supports live, always-open data connections such as streaming and WebSockets, in preview, without changing existing API specs. This lets live and AI-powered apps run through the gateway while keeping login checks and usage limits in place.

title: Step by Step guide: Build a Voice Agent That Never Goes Silent using ADK
excerpt: The open-source Agent Development Kit (ADK) and gemini-3.8-live enable developers to build responsive voice agents by implementing non-blocking tools in Python. Developers can use streaming tools to yield progress updates or background execution patterns to keep conversations fluid during long-running backend queries. Additionally, configuring response scheduling behaviors such as WHEN_IDLE, INTERRUPT, or SILENT gives developers precise control over when and how tool results are delivered into the conversation.
summary: Google shows how to build a voice agent with its open-source Agent Development Kit that keeps talking during slow tasks. It uses background or streaming tools so the conversation doesn't freeze while waiting for results.

title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
excerpt: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.
summary: Google Docs and Drive can now open, preview, and edit Markdown (.md) files directly. Developers and AI tools can work on the same file without converting it, and it still works with code tools like Git.

title: Powering the Agent Development Lifecycle with any framework, from ADK to LangChain and beyond
excerpt: The Agents CLI Extension System enables developers to use frameworks like LangChain, LangGraph, or custom enterprise stacks while retaining a unified deployment and evaluation workflow. It details a first-party LangChain template that scaffolds, runs, and deploys agents without requiring the Agent Development Kit (ADK). Additionally, it demonstrates how platform teams can author custom extensions to enforce policies such as automated software bill of materials (SBOM) scans during deployment.
summary: Google's Agents CLI now lets developers build AI agents with other frameworks, like LangChain, instead of only Google's own Agent Development Kit. The post also shows how teams can add custom rules, such as automatic security checks before deployment.

title: Optimizing a 200,000-line Python codebase overnight with Gemini 4 Argon
excerpt: How our engineering team ran Gemini 4 Argon unattended overnight with .agents/skills and /goal mode to cut in-memory session prep overhead by 40% in long sessions and speed up cold imports by 21% in Google's open-source Python Agent Development Kit (ADK).
summary: Google's engineering team used its Gemini 4 Argon AI model to improve a large open-source Python toolkit while it ran unattended overnight. The result was about 40% less setup work in long sessions and 21% faster startup.

title: Native Model Authoring for Edge with LiteRT Tensor API
excerpt: Meet the LiteRT Tensor API: giving developers native C++ control over the model graph to unify end-to-end ML computations on heterogeneous edge hardware.
summary: Google introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, which lets developers write machine learning models directly in C++. It is meant to run the full model on many different kinds of devices at the edge, such as phones and small gadgets.

title: ML Drift: Next-Gen GPU AI/ML Inference at the Edge
excerpt: Google AI Edge has introduced ML Drift, a high-performance, universal GPU compute framework designed to accelerate on-device AI and machine learning inference. By abstracting the complexities of hardware and low-level APIs—including OpenGL ES, OpenCL, Metal, and WebGPU—ML Drift enables developers to build real-time, interactive ML experiences, from sophisticated video effects to generative AI, across mobile and desktop platforms.
summary: Google AI Edge has released ML Drift, a tool that helps AI models run faster directly on phones and computers using their graphics chips. It hides the hard hardware details, so developers can more easily build real-time features like video effects and generative AI.

title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
excerpt: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. Developers can leverage these battle-tested optimization playbooks, recipes, and the Hugging Face modeling backend to efficiently scale their own workloads on TPU infrastructure.
summary: Google's TorchTPU lets people use the popular PyTorch tool to train big AI models on Google's TPU chips, without rewriting code in another language. A new TorchTitan version adds tools and tips to make these large training runs faster and more efficient.

title: Bring multimodal semantic search to the edge with EmbeddingGemma 2
excerpt: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a new 740M open-weight multimodal model that maps text, images, video, and audio into a unified vector space for privacy-first, on-device retrieval. Developers can easily integrate these capabilities cross-platform using MediaPipe Tasks or optimize fine-grained performance across CPU, GPU, and NPU accelerators with LiteRT. The model enables ultra-low-latency local solutions like search-as-you-type media retrieval, keyframe video moments finding, and zero-shot intent routing.
summary: Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, a free, open model that lets phones and devices search text, images, video, and audio by meaning, all on the device itself. This means quick, private search without sending data to the cloud.

title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics
excerpt: Gemini 4 Argon is a general-purpose physical reasoning model designed to enhance workflows across the robotics stack with advanced capabilities in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning. Developers can access and integrate Argon across Google's developer platforms—including Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, and Google Antigravity—to build and test sophisticated robotic applications. By leveraging simulation tools like MuJoCo and code-as-policies, engineers can seamlessly transition from real-world data or sketches to physically verified robot control and self-improvement workflows.
summary: Google has released Gemini 4 Argon, an AI model meant to help build robots. Developers can use it through Google's developer tools to test robot behavior in simulation before running it on real machines.

title: Evaluating AI agents: moving past the vibe check
excerpt: A practical engineering guide and reference architecture for establishing continuous evaluation pipelines for multi-turn AI agents using Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Google ADK, and OpenInference standards.
summary: Google Developers published a practical guide on testing AI agents automatically over time, instead of just checking them by feel. It shows a reference setup using Google's agent tools.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: The Developer Guide
excerpt: EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-source multimodal embedding model that maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a unified 768-dimensional space. Developers can use the sentence-transformers library to selectively load modular modality encoders—ranging from 270M to 740M parameters—to optimize memory usage. Additionally, Matryoshka Representation Learning enables dynamic dimension truncation down to 128d, significantly reducing vector database storage requirements while maintaining high retrieval performance.
summary: Google released EmbeddingGemma 2, a free, open-source model that turns text, code, images, video, and audio into a shared set of numbers so they can be compared. It can run in smaller pieces and use less storage, which helps developers save memory and space.

title: Bringing Visual Graph Debugging to Custom Edge Compilers with Model Explorer
excerpt: Google AI Edge Model Explorer now supports custom compiler intermediate representations and open-source adapters like TOSA, VGF, and PTE for on-device machine learning. Developers can leverage hierarchical graph visualization, split-pane views, and per-node trace overlays to catch export regressions and verify hardware delegation. These tools enable engineering teams to transparently debug execution graphs and pinpoint cycle-level latency bottlenecks locally.
summary: Google's Model Explorer tool can now show the internal step-by-step maps that custom compilers use for on-device AI models. Engineers can use it to spot where a model broke during conversion and find slow spots.

title: Architecting Governed, Self-Evolving AI Agents on Google Cloud
excerpt: Learn how Project Chrysalis combines Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Agent Development Kit (ADK), BigQuery, and a four-gate defense-in-depth security stack (Model Armor, Cloud KMS, Binary Authorization, and OPA) to build governed, self-evolving AI agents that remediate live production outages in 1.8 seconds.
summary: Google Developers describes Project Chrysalis, a system of AI agents built on Google Cloud that fixes live production outages in about 1.8 seconds. The agents are kept in check by several layers of security checks.

title: Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
excerpt: This post announces native PyTorch backends for vLLM and SGLang powered by TorchTPU, enabling developers to run and optimize serving workloads using familiar PyTorch tools. Built in collaboration with open-source project maintainers, these engines include optimized TPU kernel implementations, production-ready features like KV cache management with TPU Sync, and disaggregated serving. Public benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and industry-leading cost efficiency on Ironwood TPU across long-context and agentic workloads.
summary: Google announced new versions of two popular AI-serving tools, vLLM and SGLang, that run on its TPU chips using PyTorch. The post says they perform well and cost less to run on its Ironwood TPUs for long and complex AI tasks.

title: Announcing MCP support in Apigee hybrid: agentic tools that run in your own cluster

title: AWS Weekly Roundup: Amazon Polly Generative engine, TorchNeuron for Trainium, and more (October 26, 2026)
excerpt: A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 new voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice. Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo. The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the issue rather than a severity label. It ranks issues by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation currently requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future. The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon). Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer. The numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge. Last week’s launches Here are some launches that caught my attention this week. Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine n
summary: AWS launched Continuum, a service that finds code security flaws, proves which ones can be exploited, and opens fixes for a person to approve. It also released Amazon ECS Gateway, which lets network teams and app teams share how services are exposed, at no extra charge.

title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
excerpt: An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve. Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes. The plan determines the permissions For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs , then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision. Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy: Plan Work Requested scope Investigate the failure Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one read:deployment Redeploy the last known-good build Create a deployment read-write:deployment A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically. The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do: Intent : The outcome the user asks for. Work : The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it. Access : The scopes those tasks require. Enforcement : The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits. Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan. The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read: . Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless. Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions , so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have. The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits. A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions. Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions. Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use When a user approves
summary: Vercel's AI agent now investigates production problems first, using only read-only access, then shows the user a plan of what it wants to change. Changes need the user's approval of that whole plan, so people can review the fix before the agent acts.

title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
excerpt: Interfaze on Vercel 50 million requests a month Backend running on Fluid compute Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does. Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down. The backend required no infrastructure work Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox , which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up. Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box. AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else. The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality. When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there. Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK , with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence. The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long. Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up. Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part. What's next Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite , an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gat

title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
excerpt: By Roberto Perez Alcolea , Java Platform Team Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed. The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it. Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves. Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next: Does any consumer still call this method? Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations? Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact? Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign? At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds. Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally. We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions: What changed in the library’s public API? Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed? The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing. From API Changes to Consumer Impact Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive. Quasar builds on SCIP , an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently. On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change. During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings
summary: Netflix describes Quasar, a tool that indexes symbol definitions and references across its repositories using the SCIP format, so library producers can connect an API change to the exact consumer repositories that use the changed symbols. This turns compatibility warnings into evidence about observed blast radius before merging or releasing. The approach is motivated by the need for cross-repository context, including for coding agents making library changes.

title: Bringing post-quantum cryptography to geographically fenced key management
excerpt: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography . Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. For organizations with geographic requirements, resisting that threat is only half the challenge. At Cloudflare's scale, high availability requires replicating customer data across many servers across our global network. However, many data sovereignty regulations require that certain types of data be processed only within a given geographical region. We must therefore ensure the data is end-to-end encrypted such that only servers within the region have access to the plaintext. In this post, we describe the system that makes this work. The evolution of GeoKey Manager Cloudflare pioneered the concept of geo-restricted transport layer security ( TLS ) keys back in 2017 with GeoKey Manager . This gave customers control over the locations where their private TLS keys could be unwrapped on Cloudflare’s anycast network to provide stronger technical guarantees of which region their requests are decrypted into. For instance, a customer could choose to only unwrap their private keys in India. So instead of allowing decryption across Cloudflare’s entire global network, GeoKey Manager makes sure TLS signing for each customer request happens in our India network. GeoKey Manager evolved again in 2022 with ciphertext policy attribute based encryption (ABE). Instead of tying encrypted keys to a fixed set of data centers, ABE expressed geographic requirements using attributes such as country or region, like “region = European Union” or “region = Canada + United States + Mexico”. Newly authorized servers could receive matching decryption capabilities without rewrapping every customer key. That flexibility created a challenge and opportunity for the post-quantum transition. No production-ready post-quantum ABE scheme is available today, and customers do not need a large number of regions. A simpler design meets the requirement and is easier to maintain and operate. Cloudflare therefore uses hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection with two kinds of keys, out of which ML-KEM-768 is a NIST standard that also opens doors to highly sensitive customers. A regional root key is a symmetric secret tied to one region, and an application-specific key pair is derived from it for a single service, such as Gateway or Tunnel . This protects private-key material against harvest now, decrypt later while preserving regional key-use boundaries. Global ciphertext, regional key unwrapping In its new form, GeoKey Manager is the key foundation for Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions. It controls which region protected decryption keys can be used from and when. Separate workstreams determine where tunnels terminate, where traffic is inspected, how it is routed, and where plaintext processing occurs. But all
summary: Cloudflare launched a post-quantum GeoKey Manager in closed beta as part of its Data Localization Suite, ensuring customers' decryption keys can only be unwrapped by servers in an allowed geography. The system replaces earlier attribute-based encryption with a simpler design using hybrid ML-KEM-768 and X25519 protection and regional root keys, guarding against harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks while keeping key use confined to a region.

title: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning
excerpt: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-2097151/524288000 Content-Length: 1048576 Range requests are common for large objects. A video player can request bytes around a seek position instead of the whole file. A download manager can resume after an interruption. A package manager can fetch part of an artifact. A client can inspect the end of a file without downloading everything before it. The client decides whether to request a range, and Cloudflare does not change that request. Instead, Origin Range Requests changes how Cloudflare satisfies it. The range-size problem Cloudflare has supported range-request caching for years via static zone configuration. The previous implementation resembled the cache-slicing described in an nginx blog post : each client request was mapped to fixed-size ranges of the file, with the range size and file extensions configured per zone. The size of each range created a tradeoff: small ranges led to many small origin requests and memory pressure on Cloudflare from coalescing all of the requests in-memory, while large ranges caused Cloudflare to download much more data than the client requested. Updates to the range size itself would invalidate cache entries, since the size was part of the cache key. This design also meant people requesting content through our network could have unpleasant experiences accessing these files. Concurrent requests that fell inside the same range, no matter how far apart each client’s requested range was, could block each other. Our nginx-based cache also couldn’t combine range caching with concurrent streaming , a feature we built to let multiple clients read a file from cache while it's still being written. Turning both on together cut responses short, so each range had to be fully downloaded before anyone could read it, and popular files needed a separate origin fetch for every range. The extra bytes could also cross several parts of our distributed cache: from the origin to one data center, between cache tiers, and then toward the client. Every hop multiplied the waste. No value works equally well for a small seek, a sequential download, a large media file, and every origin and cache topology. Our internal cache limitations were directly exposed to customers, who should not need to understand our capabilities in-depth to have files served efficiently. Fortunately, our transition from nginx to a Pingora -based caching server created an opportunity to address the implementation problems that had forced a hard-to-use setting onto customers. Fixed-size cache chunks The fix came from something Pingora was already doing. To make it easy to resume interrupted downloads, it stores every cached file on disk in fixed-size chunks. If the cache
summary: Cloudflare replaced its fixed, per-zone range-request cache slicing with a new implementation that stores cached files in fixed-size chunks, eliminating the range-size tuning tradeoff. The result cut R2 p99 time to first byte roughly in half and reduced tiered cache traffic by about 6%. It is now available to all plans as Origin Range Requests, enabled via a Cache Rule.

title: Death to long-lived static credentials
excerpt: Fifteen years ago, TLS was something you'd use to protect the most sensitive areas of your app. Then Google, Let's Encrypt, the EFF, and others led the push for HTTPS everywhere, making encryption the default for every request. Without it, anyone between the browser and server can read and tamper with the traffic. OAuth, OIDC, DBSC, and related standards already provide building blocks for secure authentication, but standards alone do not make secure methods the norm. HTTPS needed tooling that made encryption easy and a sustained push that made it expected. Machine-to-machine authentication still resembles HTTPS in 2010, with some vendors and enterprises leading the way while long-lived static credentials remain the default for many SaaS vendors and infrastructure providers. At Vercel, we want to make fast and secure the default across the web, including in our own services and the integrations in our Marketplace. We’ve built OIDC UI , a shadcn/ui registry that gives providers trust-policy forms and token verification code. We’re expanding OIDC support across Vercel and setting new authentication requirements for Marketplace providers. Long-lived static credentials are insecure Long-lived static credentials are secrets such as API keys and database passwords that applications keep reusing, often with no expiration. As agents take on more useful work, we give them access to our systems, tools, and data through credentials that can grant permissions far beyond the task at hand. Those credentials can leak into a code repository or chat, be stolen when a service or dependency is compromised, or be exposed when prompt injection leads an agent to reveal them. However it happens, an attacker can use the credential with the permissions it grants until it expires or is revoked. Recent credential-theft and supply-chain incidents across the industry show why encryption at rest isn’t enough when malicious code can read an application’s credentials in production. Rotating exposed credentials takes time and coordination across the systems that use them, and mistakes can disrupt production. At Vercel, we’ve previously spent thousands of engineering hours on multiple, very painful key rotations out of an abundance of caution, and we never want to have to do this again. Better solutions already exist With OIDC , your application can authenticate without storing a long-lived provider key. A trusted issuer provides a signed, short-lived token identifying the application, and the receiving service verifies that token before deciding what access to grant. A stolen token stops working when it expires, limiting how long that copy can be used even if the leak goes unnoticed. Your application can obtain fresh credentials programmatically, removing the need to distribute and manually rotate a persistent provider key across the systems that use it. We’ve been prioritizing OIDC across Vercel so applications can access Blob , AI Gateway , and Sandbox without storing long-lived keys for those services. Our OIDC federation has been generally available since 2024, letting applications running on Vercel exchange Vercel-issued identity tokens for temporary AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure credentials under configured project and environment trust policies . But for developers to stop managing long-lived keys, that support has to extend to all the services their applications depend on. The rest of the web hasn’t followed We surveyed more than 1,000 SaaS vendors and found that only 8.4% supported secure authentication methods. But getting vendors to support secure authentication is only part of the problem. Even when a service offers a secure method, developers often choose a static key because it can be simpler to use. We see three main barriers to broader adoption: Tooling and setup that make secure authentication more complicated than using a static key. Added latency from fetching or exchanging tokens on the request path. Weak incentives for vendors to offer and
summary: Vercel argues that long-lived static credentials like API keys and database passwords are insecure, since leaked or stolen secrets remain usable until revoked, and that the industry needs machine-to-machine authentication to become the default as HTTPS did. The post describes Vercel's push for OIDC across its platform and Marketplace, including an OIDC UI registry and new authentication requirements for providers. title: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
excerpt: Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years. For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host. We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched. The cost of good neighbors Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management. These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota. A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota. We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised t
summary: Netflix describes single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives latency-sensitive containers their own virtual machine within the Titus platform, because shared-kernel multi-tenancy cannot fully isolate hardware resources like last-level cache and memory bandwidth. The post covers why cgroups and namespaces fall short, the alternatives considered (microVMs, gVisor, EC2), and how the mode is built on the Titus federation and autoscaling layers.

title: Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
excerpt: For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework . For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators. What a Korean user sees when they sign up The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: " By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy. " A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once: 모두 동의 (Agree to all) [필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service) [필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information) [필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas) [선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties) The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications). The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely. Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change. We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents. The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison: // Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false,
summary: Cloudflare describes achieving South Korea's ISMS-P certification after a ten-day audit by KISA-appointed auditors covering 80 controls. Beyond certification, the post explains localized Korean sign-up consent: itemized required and optional consents, and removing social sign-up paths in Korea so that every account passes through the consent gate, with country detection done via the client IP.

title: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
excerpt: Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities . AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define. Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes. Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems. Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path. For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action To show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities . Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S
summary: AWS has made AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities generally available. The service validates which code findings are actually exploitable in your environment, ranks them by business impact using an AWS context graph, and proposes fixes as pull requests that require human approval before merging.
